articles.headline: GeneBench-Pro: OpenAI's protein-folding AI breaks new ground on molecular benchmarks
articles.body: OpenAI has released GeneBench-Pro, a specialized AI model designed to advance protein structure prediction and molecular biology research. The model demonstrates significant improvements on genetic and protein benchmarking tasks, outperforming previous baselines in accuracy and inference speed. GeneBench-Pro combines language model capabilities with domain-specific training on biological datasets, allowing it to reason about amino acid sequences, predict secondary and tertiary structures, and identify functional domains with higher precision than existing tools. The model has been evaluated against standard molecular biology benchmarks and shows measurable gains in metrics like RMSE (root mean square error) for structure prediction and accuracy on protein classification tasks. Unlike general-purpose AI models, GeneBench-Pro is optimized for the specific constraints of biological data—irregular sequences, limited training examples for rare proteins, and the need for physically plausible predictions. This positions it as a tool for computational biologists, pharmaceutical researchers, and biotech companies looking to accelerate drug discovery pipelines. The release includes API access and benchmark datasets, enabling researchers to reproduce results and build on the model's capabilities.

articles.headline: vLLM's native-speed transformers backend hits native performance without the overhead
articles.body: vLLM, the open-source LLM inference engine from UC Berkeley's LLMSys lab, has released a new native-speed transformers modeling backend that lets developers run large language models at near-native speeds without custom kernels or complex optimization layers. The update simplifies the inference stack by integrating directly with HuggingFace's transformers library, eliminating the performance tax that typically comes with abstraction layers. This means faster time-to-first-token, higher throughput on batched requests, and lower latency for real-time applications like chatbots, coding agents, and API services. The backend works across multiple hardware targets—GPUs (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel) and CPUs—making it accessible for entrepreneurs running inference on cloud instances or on-prem hardware. Compared to the previous vLLM stack, this approach reduces memory overhead while maintaining compatibility with the broader transformers ecosystem, so developers don't need to retrain or reformat models. The real impact: faster inference means cheaper per-token costs, which directly improves margins for anyone monetizing API access to LLMs. Teams using vLLM for production inference can now serve more requests per GPU without upgrading hardware, or downsize their compute cluster and pocket the difference.
examples: Set up a vLLM inference server, load any HuggingFace model, and serve 10x more tokens per second than before.
Run Llama 3.1 or Mistral locally with sub-100ms latency for real-time chat applications.
Batch requests from multiple users and achieve 3-5x higher throughput on the same GPU hardware.

articles.hook: Run AI anywhere, store anywhere—the multi-cloud problem is solved.
articles.headline: SkyPilot + Hugging Face: Run AI on any cloud with zero egress costs
articles.body: SkyPilot has partnered with Hugging Face to enable a zero-egress storage solution that lets teams run AI workloads across any cloud provider while storing data on Hugging Face without paying egress fees. Previously, companies faced a brutal choice: lock their compute into one cloud to avoid data transfer costs, or pay hefty egress charges when moving data between cloud providers. This integration breaks that constraint entirely. Teams can now spin up training jobs on AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud and pull datasets directly from Hugging Face repos at no extra cost—the data transfer charges simply don't apply. The real impact: cost-sensitive AI teams and startups can now optimize for compute pricing alone, choosing whichever cloud offers the best GPU rates that day without worrying about egress penalties. This is particularly valuable for teams training large models, fine-tuning LLMs, or running inference at scale, where egress costs can easily exceed compute costs. SkyPilot handles the infrastructure orchestration and cloud-agnostic job scheduling, while Hugging Face provides the storage layer. The integration works with existing Hugging Face datasets and models, making it a plug-and-play solution for teams already using the platform.
examples: Launch a fine-tuning job on Google Cloud's cheaper GPUs, automatically pull training data from Hugging Face with zero egress fees.
Switch compute providers mid-week to catch AWS spot pricing drops—same Hugging Face storage, zero data transfer costs.
Build a multi-cloud training pipeline that picks the cheapest cloud each day without paying cloud-lock egress penalties.
